questions.prompt: Why does an AI model often propose an over-engineered 'tech stack monster' when asked to design a simple application?
options: AI models are biased toward enterprise-level codebases they were trained on.
Simple projects require more computing power from the AI to generate.
The AI is trying to ensure the application is ready for millions of users immediately.
Vanilla JavaScript is too outdated for modern AI models to write effectively.
questions.explanation: AI models reflect their training data, which includes massive amounts of professional, enterprise-grade code. This often leads them to suggest complex industrial solutions for simple beginner tasks.
correctAnswers: AI models are biased toward enterprise-level codebases they were trained on.

questions.prompt: Which of the following are considered 'Complexity Red Flags' when reviewing an AI's plan for a beginner-level MVP?
options: Requesting a PostgreSQL database for a simple list.
Using browser-native LocalStorage for data persistence.
Integrating a heavy state-management library for a three-step form.
Suggesting a single-file vanilla HTML/JS approach.
Setting up a Node.js backend for a project that could be client-side only.
questions.explanation: External databases, backend servers, and complex state libraries add layers of difficulty. For an MVP, local storage and vanilla tools are preferred to minimize points of failure.
correctAnswers: Requesting a PostgreSQL database for a simple list.
Integrating a heavy state-management library for a three-step form.
Setting up a Node.js backend for a project that could be client-side only.

questions.prompt: What is the primary danger of accepting a complex AI-generated plan with many dependencies early in a project?
options: The project will be too fast for the user to understand.
The AI will charge more for generating the complex code.
More moving parts create more points of failure, making debugging extremely difficult.
The code will only work on mobile devices.
questions.explanation: Complexity is the enemy of the beginner. Every extra library or server is something else that can break, making it much harder to figure out what went wrong when the app doesn't work.
correctAnswers: More moving parts create more points of failure, making debugging extremely difficult.

correctAnswers: Strip out all databases and servers.
Use only plain JavaScript and local CSS.
Store data in browser memory or LocalStorage.

questions.prompt: You are testing an app in the browser and notice a horizontal scrollbar appearing on the mobile view. What does this specifically indicate?
options: The layout is successfully using fluid units.
An element is wider than the viewport, causing a layout failure.
The browser is automatically zooming in for better readability.
The application has reached the maximum height allowed for a mobile screen.
questions.explanation: A horizontal scrollbar on mobile is a major indicator of a non-responsive layout; it means content is 'bleeding' off the side because it cannot shrink to fit the narrow screen width.
correctAnswers: An element is wider than the viewport, causing a layout failure.

questions.prompt: Which of the following are considered the 'big three' visual bugs to look for during a responsive layout audit?
options: The Spillover: text clipping out of its container.
The Squish: buttons becoming too small to click.
The Stack-Up: elements awkwardly overlapping.
The Ghost: elements disappearing entirely from the DOM.
The Slow-Load: images taking too long to render.
questions.explanation: Spillover, Squish, and Stack-Up are the primary visual indicators that a layout is not handling viewport changes correctly, requiring a design fix.
correctAnswers: The Spillover: text clipping out of its container.
The Squish: buttons becoming too small to click.
The Stack-Up: elements awkwardly overlapping.
